newsitem.title: USA: Clinton extends suspension of Cuban trade action.
newsitem.headline: Clinton extends suspension of Cuban trade action.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday once again delayed implementation of a law that would allow U.S. citizens to sue some foreign companies doing business in Communist-ruled Cuba.

Clinton ordered a further six-month suspension of the provision of the so-called Helms-Burton law. He said he would keep on suspending the provision as long as U.S. allies continued a stepped-up effort to promote democracy and human rights in Cuba.

"I've decided to extend for another six months the suspension of the right to file suit ...," Clinton said in a statement while on vacation in the U.S. Virgin Islands. "I would expect to continue suspending the right to file suit so long as America's friends and allies continue their efforts to promote a transition to democracy in Cuba," he said.

The provision would allow U.S. citizens, including Cubans who left after Fidel Castro took power in 1959 and are now naturalised U.S. citizens, to sue foreign companies doing business with property seized by Cuba's Communist government.

The law, enacted in March, enraged Europeans, Canadians and Mexicans who argued the United States was trying to impose its anti-Cuba trade sanctions on them. A number of countries have moved to enact laws to counter Helms-Burton and filed trade complaints to the World Trade Organisation.

Clinton, seeking to calm tensions, suspended the lawsuit provision in July for six months. He appointed Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat as a special envoy to work with U.S. allies to find common ground in trying to bring democracy to Cuba.

After a flurry of diplomatic activity by Eizenstat, who travelled to Mexico, Canada and all major European capitals, members of the European Union in December agreed to press Cuba on human rights and democracy.
That move gave Clinton room to suspend the law for at least another six months.

Clinton originally objected to key parts of the Helms-Burton law, but agreed to sign it last year after the Cuban air force in February shot down two civilian aircraft flown by anti-Castro activists. Four Miami residents were killed.

The law also bars executives of foreign companies doing business with confiscated property and their families from entering the United States. That provision has gone into effect and has been used against executives of a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.
